title: Rachel weeping (Jeremiah 31:14–16)
hook: Rachel weeps for her children, and is told "there is hope for thy future"

segments.voice: Yesterday, a letter told the exiles to plant gardens in Babylon. Your line was plant a garden there, and pray for the place. What did you do for your town? Today, from the chapters of comfort, a mother's voice. Day eight hundred five.
screen: `PLANT A GARDEN THERE, AND PRAY FOR THE PLACE.`

segments.voice: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Rachel. Jacob's beloved, the wife he waited and worked for. She died on the road, giving birth to a son, and Genesis says she was buried there, in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Generations later, Jeremiah hears her voice again. Her children are being led away into exile, and she is weeping.
screen: `A VOICE WAS HEARD IN RAMAH.` → `BURIED ON THE ROAD.` → `SHE REFUSES TO BE COMFORTED.`

segments.voice: Notice first what Rachel refuses. Comfort. Not because comfort is bad, but because her children are gone, and nothing short of their return will do. The text lets her grief stand at full height. Then God answers, and look how. He doesn't tell her she's overreacting. "Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD; and they shall come again from the land of the enemy." Thy work. Her weeping is called work, labor that will be paid. And then: "And there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border." The Jewish Publication Society's old translation puts it this way: "there is hope for thy future." Rabbinic tradition built on this. The commentator Rashi explains why Jacob buried Rachel on the road instead of in the family tomb: so that when her children were driven into exile, they would pass her grave, and she would come out and weep and plead for them. And a midrash in Lamentations Rabbah tells that when the Temple fell, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Moses each pleaded for the people, and were not answered. Then Rachel spoke, and God said: for your sake I will bring them back. So the one who refused comfort is the one whose tears are heard. Hope here isn't the opposite of grief. It's what God says to grief that refuses to quit.
screen: `SHE REFUSES TO BE COMFORTED.` · `THY WORK SHALL BE REWARDED.` · then, large: `THERE IS HOPE FOR THY FUTURE.` · then: `RACHEL'S TEARS ARE HEARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hope for someone who seems lost. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who seems far away right now: lost to addiction, to anger, to grief, to a life that's drifted off from yours. Don't argue with how hard it is. Rachel didn't. Just let yourself care about them, the way she did, without pretending. Then, quietly, set Jeremiah's words next to their name: there is hope. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. If there's one small thing that might reach them, a message, a door left open, note it for today. The bell holds the time.
Rachel weeping. The mother of the exiles, crying for her children and refusing comfort, and told: there is hope for thy future. Today's word.

Your line: there is hope. Today, keep one door open for someone who seems lost. And look back at this week: a spring, free for anyone, he stays, and he hurts with them, here, in kitchens and courts and streets, as clay in his hand, silence turned out to be impossible, plant a garden there, and pray for the place, and there is hope. Day eight hundred five.

howItsDone: These verses come near the end of the haftarah read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and people come to pray at the site known as Rachel's Tomb, near Bethlehem.

fork.setup: you're Rachel, weeping for your children in exile. people come to comfort you. what do you do?
options: accept the comfort and stop crying.
refuse to be comforted, because they're gone.
tell them to forget the children.
fork.reveal: she refused to be comforted for her children, and God answers her: there is hope, thy children shall come again.

original.note: Hebrew: there is hope, from Jeremiah 31:16 (JPS numbering).

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad verse about a mother.
what it means: Rachel's tears are called work that will be rewarded: there is hope, her children will come home.
what a scholar hears: in Lamentations Rabbah, the ancestors and Moses plead for the exiles without answer, and only Rachel's plea is heard.

notes: KJV 31:15–17 = JPS 31:14–16 (the index's numbering). The short JPS 1917 phrase 'there is hope for thy future' comes from the index hook; please verify it word for word.
'The wife he waited and worked for' and her death on the road giving birth to a son paraphrase Genesis 29 and 35.
Rashi on Genesis 48:7 (Rachel buried on the road so she could plead for exiles) and Lamentations Rabbah Petichta 24 (Rachel's plea answered) are paraphrased; please check the attributions.
